title: DMK Pushes Supreme Court Intervention as Cauvery Water Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Tamil Nadu received just 3.5 TMC of Cauvery water against a 31 TMC entitlement since June, as DMK demands court-directed release from Karnataka and a new tribunal for the Mekedatu dam dispute.
body:
• Tamil Nadu received only 3.5 TMC ft of Cauvery water between June 1 and July 22, against its Supreme Court-mandated entitlement of 31 TMC ft
  • DMK has moved the Supreme Court seeking directions for Karnataka to release water immediately and wants a tribunal constituted to address the Mekedatu dam dispute
  • Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar insists the Mekedatu project benefits Tamil Nadu, while the Centre says Karnataka doesn't need consent from lower riparian states to build it

The decades-old Cauvery river water dispute has entered its sharpest phase in years, with the opposition DMK approaching the Supreme Court to compel Karnataka to release Tamil Nadu's share of water amid a severe agricultural crisis in the state's delta region.

DMK president MK Stalin chaired a virtual meeting with party MPs in mid-July and adopted a resolution demanding the Centre intervene during Parliament's Monsoon Session. The party wants a dedicated tribunal constituted for the Mekedatu dam dispute and insists Karnataka release water "without delay, in accordance with Supreme Court directions," according to a party statement reported by ANI.

A Staggering Water Deficit

The numbers underscore the crisis. Between June 1 and July 22, Tamil Nadu received only 3.5 TMC ft (thousand million cubic feet) of Cauvery water at the interstate border at Biligundlu — roughly 11 per cent of the 31 TMC ft it was entitled to under the Supreme Court-mandated schedule for that period, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

https://x.com/haraappan/status/2083438290552926209

The shortfall has hit the Cauvery delta districts of Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, and Nagapattinam hardest, jeopardising the short-term Kuruvai paddy crop. The customary opening of the Mettur dam, normally on June 12, has been postponed indefinitely due to inadequate storage levels.

Farmer representatives from the Tamil Nadu Cauvery Farmers' Association told state Agriculture Minister R Vinoth that bilateral negotiations would "bypass the established legal protocol and contradict the Supreme Court verdict." They have demanded the state government pursue legal options instead.

Political Crosscurrents in Tamil Nadu

The Cauvery crisis has created an unusual alignment in Tamil Nadu's fractious politics. Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay of the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) favours bilateral talks with Karnataka — a stance that has drawn opposition from farmers, the DMK, and even some allies.

Yet in the Tamil Nadu Assembly, TVK and DMK backed a joint resolution in June calling for a new tribunal to counter Karnataka's push for the Mekedatu dam. AIADMK, PMK, and Left parties opposed the resolution, arguing a fresh tribunal could weaken Tamil Nadu's existing legal protections under the 2018 Supreme Court verdict.

"They will demand; no problem, we will also demand. I will also go to Delhi and tell our Members of Parliament to place the facts before everyone. Whatever the Cauvery issue is, it is our right."

— DK Shivakumar, Karnataka Chief Minister

Karnataka's Position and the Mekedatu Flashpoint

Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar has maintained that the proposed Mekedatu balancing reservoir — the most contentious element of the dispute — would actually benefit Tamil Nadu by regulating downstream water flows. He has dismissed Tamil Nadu's opposition as misplaced.

The Centre has backed Karnataka's legal position. Union Minister of State for Jal Shakti Raj Bhushan Choudhary told the Rajya Sabha in late July that the 2018 Supreme Court judgment "contains no clause requiring Karnataka to obtain clearance from the lower riparian states" before building structures on the Cauvery. The Detailed Project Report for Mekedatu has been returned to Karnataka's project authority for revision to comply with Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal standards.

What the Diaspora Should Watch

For Indians abroad with roots in Tamil Nadu or Karnataka, the dispute carries economic and emotional weight. The Cauvery delta — often called the rice bowl of Tamil Nadu — sustains millions of farming families and provides drinking water to over 20 districts. Crop failures from water shortages can drive migration and depress rural economies, affecting the very communities many diaspora members support through remittances.

What's Next

The Supreme Court is expected to hear the latest petitions seeking urgent relief for Tamil Nadu in the coming weeks. The Cauvery Water Management Authority, constituted under the 2018 verdict, has so far failed to bridge the gap between the two states. With the monsoon season in full swing and agricultural timelines closing, every week of delay narrows the window for the Kuruvai crop.

Whether Tamil Nadu's fractured political class — split between TVK's diplomatic approach and DMK's legal maximalism — can present a unified front before the court remains the key variable. Karnataka, meanwhile, shows no sign of yielding on Mekedatu, viewing it as a strategic asset for Bengaluru's growing drinking water needs.
